articles.content_orig:
After President Donald Trump rolled out the red carpet for his summit with China’s Xi Jinping last week, the U.S. and China agreed to move toward lower tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods in each direction. China’s side covers 1,619 U.S. products—stretching from beef and seafood to cosmetics and medical gear—but it leaves out a politically sensitive import: commodity soybeans.
While seed soybeans, soybean flour, and by-products from soybean processing made the cut for tariff relief, the raw soybeans American farmers sell in bulk to China—the ones at the heart of U.S-China farm tensions—did not.
Soybeans are one of the country’s biggest agricultural exports, and China is the most important buyer. The U.S. exported $16.5 billion worth of soybeans last year, making soybeans the second-largest agricultural export after corn, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture . China buys more soybeans than every other country because it has limited arable land.
That dependence has made soybeans vulnerable to swings in U.S.-China trade policy. In the years before the first Trump trade war in 2018, the American Soybean Association estimated 28% of all U.S. soybean production was shipped to China. When Beijing then imposed a 25% retaliatory tariff on U.S. soybeans in 2018, the USDA estimated farmers absorbed $9.4 billion in soybean losses, costing Iowa $1.2 billion and Illinois $1.3 billion.
The Midwest bears the brunt of this pressure. Illinois and Iowa are the country’s two largest soybean producers, followed by Minnesota, Indiana, and Nebraska. North and South Dakota, Missouri, and Ohio are also major growers. Soybeans are traded in export and national markets, so weaker Chinese demand can hurt farmers by driving down the cash prices they receive at local grain facilities.
That helps explain why Trump focused on soybeans in his dealmaking with Beijing. In November, he struck a deal with Xi under which China committed to buying at least 25 million metric tons of soybeans in 2026, 2027, and 2028. After he met Xi in May, the first time a U.S. president visited China since 2017, the White House announced China agreed to buy at least $17 billion in agricultural products on top of those prior soybean commitments.
For all of soybeans’ importance to American farmers, China has another supplier: Brazil.
Unlike with products such as beef, whose quality varies depending on the country of origin, bulk soybeans are interchangeable and ultimately end up crushed in troughs for livestock feed, according to Ker Gibbs, former president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Shanghai. “They go into pig feed, so it’s not like the pigs are really gonna see a big difference between American soybeans and Brazilian soybeans,” he told Fortune .
Brazil had already overtaken the U.S. as China’s largest soybean supplier over a decade ago, but recent trade tensions have widened the gap. USDA said 71% of China’s soybean imports came from Brazil , and its agricultural attaché in Beijing reported last year that Brazil’s share had continued to grow “at the expense of the United States,” helped by cheaper prices.
“They definitely want to keep Brazil warm, and so they don’t want to suddenly shift everything over to the U.S.,” Gibbs told Fortune about China excluding commodity soybeans from the list. “They’re leaving the door half closed.”
Leaving raw soybeans outside the tariff relief package also gives Beijing a holstered weapon, according to Usha Haley, a professor at Wichita State University who has studied Chinese trade strategy.
“That gives China a bargaining chip for subsequent talks, and, of course, this is about leverage,” Haley told Fortune . “They offer enough to demonstrate that they are moving on things, that they are present, but they always hold something back economically and politically for the next round.”
China doesn’t need to stop buying U.S. soybeans entirely for that pressure to work, having bought 1 million tons of them ahead of the Trump-Xi summit.
“Commercial purchasing and negotiating leverage can operate simultaneously,” Haley said. She ‘said’ China just has to keep access to its soybean market uncertain and expensive for farmers operating on thin margins. “Uncertainty also has a cost.”

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's Zelenskiy says North Korea prepares to deploy another 10,000 troops to Russia
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's Zelenskiy says North Korea prepares to deploy another 10,000 troops to Russia
articles.content_orig:
Antonia is a reporter based in Kyiv who covers Ukraine and Russia. She was shortlisted for Best Early Career Journalist in the Freelance Journalist Awards 2025
Robert Brovdi sets a box of Fortnum & Mason tea bags down next to a digital counter.
The white number reads 167: the Russian soldiers – or, as Mr Brovdi calls them, “worms” – killed that day.
The rate of attrition is intensifying rapidly, the commander of Ukraine’s drone forces and one of the chief architects of modern warfare says.
His troops have seen a 25 per cent increase in Russian casualties since August as more of the Kremlin’s foot soldiers approach the front lines .
It is his view, shared by Ukrainian military intelligence, that Vladimir Putin will imminently launch a fresh round of mobilisation to break the current stalemate.
Some 300,000 will arrive in the coming months, he estimates, in an attempt to capture the rest of the Donbas region.
“Putin will send his serfs onto the front line, and they will drop dead in even greater numbers than right now,” he says, confident that his forces can pick them off from above as the trees and bushes lose their foliage.
He picks up the counter, which has now reached 185.
“By the time we had exchanged a few sentences, 18 more b-----ds have already ended their stories in the ‘special military operation’.”
He boasts that his forces are now killing the equivalent of one enemy battalion per day.
“We are ready to welcome these limitless portions of stewed meat.”
Our interview takes place in an underground command post at a secret location in eastern Ukraine.
A team from The Telegraph was driven there on the morning Ukraine launched its largest-ever drone attack on Moscow.
It was the final day of elections in Russia, after which many experts predicted Putin would escalate his war on Ukraine and, in some respects , Europe.
The bunker is dimly lit by a bank of screens on the walls showing live footage recorded by drones hovering over the 745 miles of front line.
The tea bags are another feature, one he will turn to later to make a point about British drone prowess – or its lack thereof.
Before the war, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces and founder of the elite “Magyar’s Birds” drone unit was a wealthy international grain trader and art patron with no military experience to speak of.
An ethnic Hungarian from Uzhhorod in western Ukraine, with the call sign Magyar – “the Hungarian” – Mr Brovdi enlisted in Ukraine’s territorial defence just before the war began. Later, while serving in the 206th territorial defence battalion, he became one of the first to envision the role that drones could play in the conflict.
Mr Brovdi deployed rudimentary commercial drones to reconnoitre Russian positions after he’d bought an unmanned aerial vehicle ( UAV ) as a gift for his son.
The breakthrough, which took place in summer 2022 in Kherson, saw him sending coordinates to a nearby artillery team. But it was not long before his troops were experimenting with attaching their own munitions to the drones, which they also began manufacturing themselves.
Those improvised experiments, borne largely of desperation and a lack of resources, would prove to be the crucible from which Ukraine’s sophisticated drone warfare apparatus emerged.
The commander’s mordant wit and distinctive parlance (Russian soldiers are khrobaky , worms or bugs, while Ukrainians are pest-controlling “birds”) have transformed him into an icon of the war effort. But he has also brought to the battlefield the same mathematical and business acumen that once served him in the world of commerce, turning Ukraine’s drone strategy into a rigorous data-led exercise.
His pivotal role has also turned him into a priority target for the Kremlin. To meet him requires a series of precautions, starting with a journey to an undisclosed location in a blacked-out van after being stripped of all electronic devices, followed by a descent into the underground command post.
On a wall at its entrance, the sleek black carcass of a real Shahed drone, gutted for its parts, is mounted like the spoils of a hunt. Inside, hundreds of live first-person feeds from the battlefield line the walls on vast screens. Combing the terrain from above, lone Russian troops are stalked through the landscape and their vehicles obliterated. An electronic ledger on the wall tallies the number of enemy soldiers, artillery and weapons systems destroyed in real time.
The feeds are interspersed with maps of St Petersburg and Moscow, the latter visited only hours earlier by hundreds of Ukrainian drones – an explosive closing ceremony for Russia’s three-day parliamentary elections.
Despite the scale and ferocity of the nighttime attacks, Mr Brovdi showed no trace of fatigue. He dons a black cap embroidered with one of his slogans – Moskva lyazhe , roughly “Moscow will fall” – as he expounds on the role of his forces’ “deep strikes” in bringing the war home to Russia.
“In all of its previous wars, Russia waged them in such a way that its civilian population did not feel directly affected by the war,” says the commander.
“In 2026, this situation has been changed by our freedom-loving Ukrainian ‘birds’. Deep operations have effectively destroyed the concept of having a safe rear across the entire European part of Russia.”
This year, expanded strikes on Russia’s oil industry and commercial targets such as warehouses belonging to e-commerce giants Ozon and Wildberries have reached as far as 3,000km – almost 1,900 miles – from the Ukrainian border.
Kyiv claims that its attacks, which have hit all but five of Russia’s 32 biggest oil refineries, have sent total oil refining capacity plummeting by 45 per cent, offering some leverage to its leaders in talks. Last week, Donald Trump prematurely announced a limited energy truce on both sides, though Russia has refused such a moratorium.
“The appearance in 2026, however illusory, of even a faint prospect of a dialogue about an energy truce is the direct result of the Ukrainian ‘birds’ and Ukrainian pilots,” Mr Brovdi says.
But when it comes to the prospects of the broader US-Ukraine-Russia negotiating track, recently revived with consecutive trips to Moscow and Kyiv by the US president’s envoys, he harbours few hopes: “From a military point of view, I do not believe in an end to the war even if a ceasefire agreement is reached.”

Ukraine has struggled to defend itself against the drones, which move significantly faster and at higher altitudes than earlier generations and have struck petrol stations, warehouses, border crossings, railway infrastructure, depots, postal services and more.

“They work in close cooperation with front-line troops and have successfully started to launch jet-powered anti-Shahed systems and shoot down drones,” the commander said.

articles.title_zh: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: Spectacle-heavy Trump-Xi summit was more about domestic messaging
articles.content_orig:
Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses.
Now that the second Trump-Xi summit of the year is over, it's clear the show was aimed more at home than reaching tangible outcomes . Is agreeing to talk enough?
The $30 billion tariff rollback released Monday morning Beijing time reads like the perfect shopping list.
American consumers get to buy cheaper curtains, sports equipment and Christmas lights. Chinese get a discount on U.S. beef, soymeal and other agricultural products. American ice cream is even on the list.
It's the most detailed outcome so far of the summit last week between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C.
The official readouts otherwise did not make much headway on major issues, beyond agreeing to keep talking and extending a trade truce — which keeps tariffs lower and rare earths flowing — for another two months.
"Both sides are signaling not to each other, but to their own sides," Cameron Johnson, Shanghai-based senior partner of consultancy Tidal Wave Solutions, told me on Monday.
"The reality is neither side can do a whole lot in technology without the other," he said, "so it's important that both sides signal that to their own apparatus: It's OK to have some competition."
Over the weekend, The Information reported , citing sources, that the Chinese government has signaled it could allow some domestic companies like ByteDance and Alibaba to buy Nvidia's chip built for high-end professional computers. While the U.S. has agreed to let Nvidia sell some less advanced chips to China, there have been few signs that Chinese companies were allowed to buy them amid Beijing's push for self-sufficiency.
In Beijing's readout of talks with Trump, Xi acknowledged "healthy" competition with the U.S. was possible, without confrontation. Both countries have planned discussions on AI in coming weeks.
"I think the top priority for both leaders is to maintain domestic stability and prosperity," said Hai Zhao, a director of international political studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, a state-affiliated think tank.
"And if the two top economies are stable and growing, that is, I think, the best contribution to global stability and prosperity," he told me on Friday.
Both countries are seeing growth concentrated in tech-related sectors, also known as the "K-shaped" economy. AI's development poses the same risks to jobs and national security.
The U.S. and Chinese readouts also signaled some alignment on limiting Iran's nuclear weapon capabilities, and agreed "no country or institution can be allowed to impose tolls on international waterways."
"Even though China [and the] U.S. may have different strategic goals in different regions, however, from time to time, they share the same mutual interest," Zhao said, pointing to the need for stable trade flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.
"In many ways they can working towards the same goal by not necessarily working with each other," he said. "I call this passive cooperation."
Zhao also hopes U.S. and European scrutiny on China's exports can be resolved by encouraging Chinese companies to invest.
While the U.S. and China have released more details on the Board of Trade, less is yet known about the Board of Investment.
The question is whether it will get enough airtime in a packed political calendar.
Trump faces the midterm elections in early November. Xi will oversee a plenary meeting in late October aimed at unifying the ruling Communist Party of China. The two presidents are also planning to meet: in Shenzhen in November and in Miami in December.
"After eight turbulent years spanning trade war 1.0 to trade war 2.0, signs of stability carry real weight for domestic audiences and entrepreneurs, who are concerned about external environment," Macquarie's Chief China Economist, Larry Hu, said in a report Sunday.
"In reality," he said, "the U.S.–China relationship also anchors much of China's broader diplomacy with the rest of the world."

articles.title_orig: UAE confirms Israel PM Netanyahu’s visit to Abu Dhabi
articles.title_zh: UAE confirms Israel PM Netanyahu’s visit to Abu Dhabi
articles.content_orig:
The United Arab Emirates has confirmed that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met with President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan during a visit to the country over the weekend.
The confirmation late on Monday came a day after the Israeli leader made the secret trip to the UAE capital, Abu Dhabi. The visit came a month before Israeli elections and amid controversy over reports alleging that Bin Zayed, known as MBZ, had warned Netanyahu that a major Hamas operation was likely just ahead of the attack on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.
“During the meeting, the two sides discussed bilateral relations between the UAE and Israel and ways to strengthen and develop them,” the official Emirates News Agency, WAM, reported on Monday. The meeting was earlier reported in the Israeli press.
Palestinian fighters killed at least 1,195 people in southern Israel during the attack and took around 250 captive. Israel’s response developed into a genocidal war on Gaza, in which at least 73,669 Palestinians have been killed.
Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported on September 9 that the UAE president spoke to Netanyahu on the phone about 10 days before the attack, warning him of a threat made by then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar that he was preparing a “huge surprise”.
Bin Zayed had previously alerted Israel’s Shin Bet intelligence agency, the Haaretz report said.
Netanyahu’s office has denied that the prime minister received information ahead of the attacks.
Netanyahu said the following day that he would sue Haaretz, calling its report “fabricated” and “politically motivated”.
Relations between Israel and the UAE have warmed since the UAE signed the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020, which normalised ties between Israel and a number of Arab states.
United States Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said in May that Israel had deployed Iron Dome air defence batteries and personnel to the UAE to help defend against potential Iranian attacks.
Israel’s Channel 12 first reported on Netanyahu’s trip to the UAE over the weekend. Shin Bet said on Monday that it had filed a complaint with Israel’s military censor, saying the report endangered the prime minister and exposed the intelligence agency’s operational methods, The Associated Press news agency reported.
The allegation that the prime minister ignored a warning regarding the Hamas attack comes as Netanyahu is trying to secure his position in the upcoming Knesset elections, scheduled for October.
He has been trailing in the polls, facing a fierce challenge from former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.

PLYMOUTH, Mass. — Lindsay Clancy's legal team and Massachusetts prosecutors have agreed to delay defense attorney Kevin Reddington’s motion to investigate the lone holdout juror in her mistrial, his attorney Edward Paltzik told Fox News' Kayleigh McEnany Monday.
"The DA and Reddington consent to adjourn the motion to investigate Michael," Paltzik said. "If Judge Sullivan signs an order today, much of it could be adjourned. Either way, a status conference is still likely. But the motion about Michael is likely not on tomorrow."
Clancy attorney Kevin Reddington, however, fired back a short time later in a fiery statement of his own, calling Paltzik's statement "pure nonsense" while conceding that he and county prosecutors had agreed to a continuation as a "professional courtesy" to local counsel now working with the holdout juror.
A final decision is subject to Judge William Sullivan, but the judge has not yet announced a decision one way or the other. The delay agreement comes as the juror's new local counsel informed the parties that he does not have access to impounded information necessary to prepare a response.

Michael P. Desronvil, left, the lone holdout juror who forced a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy case, has retained an attorney who once represented President Donald Trump. As is professional courtesy, both the government and I agreed to continue this specific motion to a later date at their request."
He said the motion "remains active, fully alive, and is currently pending a ruling."
"We will not allow a publicity-seeking opportunist to twist simple courtroom courtesy into a victory that does not exist," he added.
Michael P. Desronvil, the lone holdout juror in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial, which ended in a mistrial. (Fugitive TV)
The terms adjourned and continued are similar but have distinct meanings.
"Adjournment generally signifies that something like a hearing is off indefinitely especially because no date is specified," explained retired Massachusetts Judge Carol Erskine. "A continuance is a simple request by a party or two parties to get a new date. [Reddington] objects because adjournment is a misrepresentation of what is happening."

The hearing was expected to cover Reddington's motion to hold an inquiry into the holdout, Michael Desronvil, as well as a double jeopardy motion seeking to dismiss the charges instead of holding a retrial.

EAGAN, Minn. â Even something believed to be the best decision can be tremendously difficult.
Such is the case for Vikings General Manager Nolan Teasley and Head Coach Kevin O'Connell in opting to trade J.J. McCarthy to the Giants in exchange for a 2027 fifth-round draft pick.
O'Connell called Monday "a tough day," and Teasley emphasized the human aspect of the transaction in their respective press conferences with Twin Cities media members.
"These types of decisions for me are never easy because the person is important," Teasley said. "I think he was an important person to this organization. I enjoyed my time getting to know J.J. I want the best for him, and I hope he succeeds in the future."
O'Connell noted nothing about the business decision changes the way he feels about McCarthy or the "hopes" he has for the 23-year-old quarterback moving forward. He believes New York â who recently lost starting QB Jaxson Dart for the season to a knee injury â presents a favorable opportunity for McCarthy.
"As I told him, I'll be pulling for him like crazy, to see him go and do well and apply a lot of the things we've talked about over his period of time here," O'Connell said.
He emphasized the amount of time he's spent with McCarthy since the Vikings drafted him 10 th overall in 2024.
"I care about him. I have tremendous respect for him as a player, a person," O'Connell said. "I've just had a chance to spend time with him this morning, which was emotional. Our relationship means a lot to me. I believe it means a lot to him, and I was just really thankful to have that time 1-on-1 with him.
"These situations are never easy. From a standpoint of being the head coach, you understand hard decisions in the NFL. I understand them firsthand, going back a long way for me personally," O'Connell continued. "It's always going to be about the relationship. It's always going to be about investing in all these players so much and understanding their families are involved with that."
Below are additional takeaways from Monday's media sessions with Teasley and O'Connell.

1. Timing & return of trade
O'Connell acknowledged the importance of relationships with players and their families while also recognizing the ultimate business of leading a pro team.
"You understand the decisions in the NFL that have to be made in the best interest in the organization," O'Connell said, "and you have a responsibility, and that's why I credit Nolan throughout â¦ just his ability to handle situations with so much tact and thought, always thinking forward on building our team."
Teasley confirmed that McCarthy never requested a trade, but he declined to specify exactly when conversations around a potential transaction began. He did note that this specific situation â timing, scenario and compensation â prompted the trade to happen how and when it did.
"You have to recognize when a different situation or a new opportunity presents itself that it has the opportunity to present better outcomes," Teasley said. "When the situation with the Giants presented itself, we spoke internally â that's coaches, myself, the personnel staff, ownership â everyone came together. Just in terms of where we are and in terms of our roster, where it is currently â¦ and what we might want to do in the future.
"Ultimately, we came to the conclusion that this was the best path forward and the best decision for the Minnesota Vikings," he added.
Teasley later said things "recently came together" to make the trade.
"We got to the point where the return made sense for us now to get an asset that, in all honesty, is going to help us in the future, or it could help us this season," he said. "So to have another asset that can help us continue to build, because the season and this roster [is] going to constantly evolve, and today's another example of that."
2. Exhausted development plan
Considering McCarthy only made 10 starts, O'Connell was asked about the trade through the lens of: Was there anything else that could have been done to bring McCarthy along?
He said the organization emptied the tank in its efforts to develop the 23-year-old.
"We tried to do everything we could to collaborate with a plan for [him] among coaches, among everybody in this building to try to put him in position to develop and grow," the coach said. "And I do think, you know, I do think he did. I do think he did develop and grow.
"And I think he improved. I think he improved this offseason," he added. "But at the same time, you're always going to look inward and look at it [like the] circumstances, they are what they were and are. But what could we have done differently? And J.J. and I talked about that this morning of, you know, like 'Do I wish I took him out of that first preseason game earlier? You know, whatever it may be, like that's where your mind goes, and I think it's a good question."
3. Murray's trajectory & QB room
Minnesota kept four quarterbacks on its initial 53-man roster, achieving its goal of building a deep and competitive room. Without McCarthy, Teasley maintained there's "a lot of belief" in the position.
He cited Kyler Murray's potential in the offense and is "still looking forward to that coming to fruition" after he took some steps forward Sunday in his first full game since October 2025.
Teasley also highlighted Carson Wentz's ability "to step in and win football games" and noted that Max Brosmer's development is important to the organization.
O'Connell elaborated on Murray and the offense trying to mesh.
"Look, we've seen Kyler play 11 snaps in one game and played against a good defense on the road yesterday. There's a lot of things beyond Kyler that we need to improve, including myself, and we're going to do that, and we're going to ascend as an offense," O'Connell said. "I believe in our guys. I believe in where we can get to as a team, and I just love the fact that collectively we're able to come together and find a way to win football games."

articles.content_orig:
Television Business Editor
The MTV Video Music Awards scored their largest audience in more than a decade on Sunday night.
The awards averaged 8.43 million viewers on CBS and MTV (including an encore on the latter), up by 51 percent from last year’s 5.6 million — which was also a multi-year high. Sunday’s audience (subject to adjustments when Nielsen adds its big data component) was the biggest for the VMAs since the 2015 show brought in more than 12 million people across multiple channels.
The VMAs also had their best performance among adults 18-49 (2.66 million in that age range) since 2018; among adults 25-54 (3.11 million) since 2019; and among adults 18-34 (1.09 million) since 2020.
Madonna — who also opened the show with a performance featuring Charli XCX and Sabrina Carpenter — was the night’s big winner with seven awards. Taylor Swift won video of the year for “The Fate of Ophelia” and also was given the first Artist Director award for musical artists who also direct videos.
The awards, hosted by Snoop Dogg, also featured tributes to Dolly Parton and George Michael. Nirvana was awarded the Video Vanguard honor.
The VMAs also benefited from what was likely a very large NFL lead-in. The awards peaked at 15 million viewers for Madonna’s opening number, which directly followed a game-winning field goal for the Baltimore Ravens over the Dallas Cowboys (who are perennially among the NFL’s biggest TV draws). The 2025 VMAs also had a strong NFL lead-in (23.9 million viewers), but the Ravens-Cowboys audience has a good chance of passing that mark.
CBS accounted for 7.61 million viewers, or 90 percent of the total audience. MTV’s simulcast drew 686,000 viewers, and the replay chipped in 142,000 more.
On social media, the awards accounted for 159 million video views across platforms, up 8 percent year to year.

articles.title_zh: AirPods Pro 3 vs AirPods 5: Three reasons to go Pro
articles.content_orig:
Apple debuted the all-new AirPods 5 this month, and they bring ANC to lower prices than ever before. If you’re shopping for AirPods, however, there are still several reasons you might want to opt for the more expensive AirPods Pro 3.
AirPods are one of Apple’s most personal products. The fit can vary dramatically between different people depending on the size of their ears. AirPods 5 offer an open-ear design, so they rest on the inside of your ear. AirPods Pro, meanwhile, offer a more traditional in-ear design with ear tips.
Personally, I find AirPods Pro to be more comfortable than AirPods 5. They’re also more secure for me, so I’m less worried they’ll fall out of my ears.
One of the key differentiators between AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods 5 is that AirPods Pro 3 offer built-in heart rate monitoring capabilities. During a workout, AirPods Pro can measure your heart rate to provide additional fitness metrics.
If you wear an Apple Watch, AirPods Pro 3 work along with your Apple Watch to ensure you get the most accurate data possible. Apple’s algorithms monitor the data from AirPods Pro and Apple Watch, and factor in the type of workout you’re doing, to use the most consistent data possible. For example, if you’re lifting weights and the Apple Watch ends up at an awkward angle on your wrist, AirPods Pro 3 will step in to provide more accurate data.
Furthermore, in iOS 27, Apple brought GymKit to the iPhone, so you can use iPhone and AirPods to get an Apple Watch-style experience … but without wearing a watch. Learn more about this change in Zac’s full coverage .
AirPods Pro 3 offer a range of hearing health features that aren’t available on AirPods 5. This includes:
With the Hearing Test feature, you can take a 5-minute test to identify if you have hearing loss. Apple’s Hearing Aid feature, meanwhile, is a clinical-grade hearing aid that uses the results of your test to craft a sound profile for your needs. Finally, Hearing Protection, can help prevent exposure to loud environmental noise.
There are other reasons to choose AirPods Pro over AirPods 5, including longer battery life, even better ANC, and a more capable charging case. The difference in ANC, in particular, is notable: Apple says AirPods Pro 3 offer 3x more Active Noise Cancellation than AirPods 5.

articles.title_orig: Pope urges Europe to defend multilateralism as global order crumbles
articles.title_zh: Pope urges Europe to defend multilateralism as global order crumbles
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV has praised multilateralism as “the best defence against the desire for dominance” in a speech in the French city of Metz.
The pontiff lamented a world marked by conflict, from war and hunger to deteriorating personal relations, describing an “increasingly uncivilised” climate. He also criticised the “lies and deception” he said were fuelling growing distrust between citizens and governments.
Speaking in Schuman’s hometown, a city closely associated with European reconciliation, Leo said Europe could break this vicious cycle by reaffirming its commitment to the rule of law and dialogue.
"Europe can break this cycle by upholding the principle of respect for others, which it has successfully cultivated and maintained, having demonstrably shown over the past eighty years that it is possible to express divergent opinions, demands, and interests through dialogue rather than confrontation," he said.
The Pope delivered his address in French in the presence of French President Emmanuel Macron, who is due to attend a Mass with Leo later on Tuesday.
Although the Pope did not explicitly mention Russia's war against Ukraine, he condemned what he qualified as a new “pointless massacre" on European soil.
"It is necessary to engage in patient dialogue, to show courage in negotiations, and to be willing to compromise on certain positions for the greater good of peace."
Leo XIV also urged Europeans to remember the continent’s Christian roots, describing Europe as more than a geographical entity and instead a “cultural and historical reality”.
“We cannot speak of Europe, then, without mentioning Christianity,” he said, arguing that its traditions could coexist with efforts to shape the continent’s future.
Europe, he added, “has flourished and progressed when it was able to draw on the best aspects of its past and reinvent them in new and creative ways through encounter with others.”
The choice of Metz as the venue for the Pope’s address was rich in European symbolism.
Located in France’s northeastern Lorraine region, close to the German border, the city is closely associated with one of the founding figures of European integration, Robert Schuman. He opened his law practice there in 1912, and launched his political career in the city.
But Metz’s history also reflects the conflicts that shaped modern Europe. The city changed hands several times between France and Germany and was annexed by Nazi Germany in 1940, following France’s defeat and occupation.
The Élysée Palace said Monday’s programme was designed to highlight the “European and cross-border dimension” of Lorraine, a region at the crossroads of several countries with a shared and often painful history of war.
EU leaders and the heads of European institutions were invited to attend the event, although only a handful joined French President Emmanuel Macron, including representatives from Monaco, Andorra and Luxembourg.
The gathering also brought together representatives of different faiths, including France’s chief rabbi, Haïm Korsia, and Chems-Eddine Hafiz, rector of the Grand Mosque of Paris.
